newsitem.title: GERMANY: Berlin court jails "disturbed" Bosnian for hijack.
newsitem.headline: Berlin court jails "disturbed" Bosnian for hijack.

text.p: A German court on Friday sentenced a Bosnian refugee to seven years in prison for hijacking an Austrian Airlines plane in January en route from Berlin to Vienna.

Salko Loncaric, a 40-year-old Bosnian roofer who has been living in Germany since 1992, had confessed at the start of the trial, saying his aim was to secure a German residency permit. His visa at the time was due to expire the following week.

The court ordered Loncaric to begin serving his sentence in a psychiatric clinic. He had admitted that he had been emotionally disturbed and under the influence of alcohol when he stormed the plane's cockpit.
A psychiatrist submitted a report to the court diagnosing Loncaric as suffering from paranoid psychosis.
Judge Nils Neelsen called the defendant selfish and said his imminent deportation did not excuse the hijack.
"The accused created an atmosphere of fear and horror for the passengers on board," Neelsen read from his decision, at which point Loncaric broke into tears.

Loncaric forced the pilot at knifepoint to return to Berlin. The January 7 incident ended without violence when police entered the plane from the rear and pushed Loncaric out of an open door on to the tarmac at Berlin's Tegel airport.
As he waited in the courtroom for the judges to appear, Loncaric began banging his head against the wood-panelled walls of the room until a bailiff and his interpreter led him out.

He was brought back into the courtroom after television cameramen were asked to leave. When asked if he wished to speak before the verdict was read, Loncaric said: "I feel very bad. I wish I could just take some poison and end all of this."

Loncaric had testified during the trial that he had concealed a kitchen knife in his jacket, a 45-cm (18-inch) long wooden baton in his waistband, and another bat and 18 fist-size stones in his carry-on luggage.
The incident sparked accusations that the western Berlin airport, which employs a private security company, was cutting costs at the expense of passenger safety.
The airport, which was known for its stringent security during the Cold War, denied the accusations.
The plane, a McDonnell-Douglas MD-80, was only one-quarter full with 28 passengers and five crew members. The passengers included German, Austrian and Japanese citizens.
State prosecutors had pressed for a nine-year sentence, while Loncaric's defence argued for two years on probation.
